Research / Biological risk & resilience

Evolution continues
after design.

We examine how biological systems change over time, and what that means for safeguard reliability, environmental interactions, and preparedness.

All research↗
01

Containment reliability

How does containment reliability change over time? We study the evolutionary and environmental conditions that inform review intervals and reassessment.

↗02

Biological safeguard stability

Will a built-in safety mechanism retain its intended function as a population evolves? We examine the effects of mutation, selection, and fitness trade-offs on safeguard durability.

↗03

Spillover risk

What changes when an organism encounters an unintended setting? We model persistence and interaction in the context of ecological communities and host responses.

↗04

Ecological & host interactions

How do interactions alter the risk picture? We examine host responses, microbiome perturbations, ecological competition, and effects that emerge at the system level.

↗05

Evolutionary early warning

Which observations should prompt a closer look? We connect evolutionary trajectories with monitoring priorities and evidence for timely reassessment.

A common language

Key concepts.
Clear meanings.

Mathematical models make their assumptions explicit. A shared vocabulary helps connect forecasts with decisions.

Biocontainment+

Strategies to prevent engineered organisms from persisting in unintended environments, including genetic, chemical, and physical barriers.

Kill Switches+

Genetic circuits designed to eliminate cells when specific conditions are met or when they escape containment, using toxin-antitoxin systems or essential gene dependencies.

Evolutionary Stability+

The capacity of engineered genetic circuits to resist degradation or escape through mutation and selection over microbial generations.

Auxotrophy+

Engineering organisms to require specific nutrients not available in natural environments, creating a metabolic dependency for survival.

Gene Drive+

Genetic elements that bias inheritance to increase their frequency in populations, with potential for rapid ecological spread.
